growth_story.headline: Hurricanes in 2017 and the pandemic in 2020 cut income per person deeply; a tourism-led rebuild has lifted it, but not back to its 2011 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Sint Maarten peaked in 2011, and in 2025 it was still 10.2 percent below that peak and lower than in 2009, the first year of the record. From 2010 to 2017 growth averaged -1.2 percent a year: after gains in 2010 and 2011, income per person slipped every year, and the IMF described years of weak growth, with little private investment in 2015 beyond an airport expansion. That era ended with Hurricanes Irma and Maria in September 2017, which damaged most of the island's infrastructure; income per person fell 9.3 percent in 2017 and 8.5 percent in 2018. Since 2018 growth has averaged 0.9 percent a year, in large swings: a 9.1 percent rebound in 2019, a 14.6 percent fall in 2020 when air travel collapsed in the pandemic, and a 12.4 percent jump in 2022. Since 2023 growth has been steadier, between 1.6 and 2.3 percent a year, carried by stayover tourism and by rebuilding paid for through a Trust Fund financed by the Netherlands, including a new airport terminal.

threads.title: Weak years before the storms
threads.text: Before 2017 the economy was already stalling. The IMF described years of weak growth that trailed the island's neighbours, with no major private investment in 2015 apart from an airport expansion.

threads.title: Rebuilding through the Trust Fund
threads.text: Recent growth has come from tourism and from rebuilding paid for by the Trust Fund set up after Hurricane Irma, including the new airport. The IMF expects this rebuilding to wind down and be replaced by private and government building. In 2023 the IMF said the island still had further to go to reach its levels from before Irma.

since_last_year.text: In September 2025 the IMF board ended its 2025 review, pointing to doubts about how well the government can carry out projects once the Trust Fund closes. In December 2025 the World Bank closed its airport rebuilding project, saying the restored terminal leaves room for years of growth in demand.

growth_story.tension: The IMF reports the economy as a whole growing in 2014, 2015 and 2024, but in the data income per person fell 0.7 percent in 2014 and 2.0 percent in 2015, and rose only 1.6 percent in 2024. The sources do not explain the gap. It may come from population growth or from revisions to the figures.
